title: Which one's better?
goal: Compare two phones with Sēf: better, cheaper, more expensive, lighter, faster
tip: To compare, use the afʿal shape + min 'than': rkhīṣ → arkhaṣ 'cheaper', ghāli → aghla 'more expensive', zēn → azyan or aḥsan 'better'. It never changes for gender: hādha aḥsan, hādhi aḥsan. Say 'by how much' with b-: aghla b-miya 'a hundred more'.
grammar: Comparative afʿal + min: aḥsan min 'better than'; the same form for masculine and feminine
dialogue: سيف، أي واحد أحسن؟ هذا ولا هذاك؟
Sēf, ay wāḥid aḥsan? hādha walla hādhāk?
Sēf, which one's better? This one or that one?
هذا أحسن من هذاك، بس أغلى
hādha aḥsan min hādhāk, bas aghla
This one's better than that one, but it's more expensive.
b-miya bas. w il-kāmira ḥaggah azyan
Only a hundred. And its camera is better.
But that one's lighter and smaller.
صح. شو تبي، أرخص ولا أسرع؟
ṣaḥḥ. shu tabi, arkhaṣ walla asraʿ?
True. What do you want, cheaper or faster?
Faster. OK, I'll take this one, it's worth it.
items: never changes: hādhi aḥsan (this one (f.) is better); aḥsan min = better than
from ghāli; aghla b-miya = a hundred more
from zēn; aḥsan is more common
for a feminine thing: ay waḥda?
it's worth it; he deserves it
ma yistāhil = it's not worth it

title: A bigger size?
goal: Try on a shirt with Sēf: too tight, too loose, another size or colour
tip: Sizes compare like prices: akbar 'bigger', aṣghar 'smaller'; add shwayy for 'a bit': aṣghar shwayy. Colours have the same shape (aḥmar 'red', azrag 'blue') but they aren't comparatives: they change for a feminine noun (ḥamra, zarga), while akbar and aḥla never change.
grammar: Comparatives of size (akbar, aṣghar shwayy); colours look like comparatives but agree
dialogue: Sēf, this shirt's tight on me.
This one's bigger, but it's a bit loose.
Try the blue one, it's a bit smaller.
الأزرق؟ ما أحب الأزرق. عندهم أحمر؟
il-azrag? ma aḥibb il-azrag. ʿindhum aḥmar?
The blue? I don't like blue. Do they have red?
هيه، بس والله الأزرق لايق عليك، أحلى من الأحمر
hē, bas wallāh il-azrag lāyig ʿalēk, aḥla min il-aḥmar
Yes, but honestly the blue suits you, it's nicer than the red.
items: from kbīr; akbar minni = older than me
you'll also hear sāyz (سايز), from English
to a woman: lāyig ʿalēch (لايق عليج)

title: The best one in the shop
goal: Buy a perfume for your mum in the souq: ask for the best, react to the price, bargain
tip: afʿal before a noun means 'the most': aḥsan wāḥid 'the best one', aghla wāḥid 'the most expensive one', aḥsan shay 'the best thing'. No il- is needed: hādha aḥsan wāḥid ʿindi 'this is the best one I've got'.
grammar: Superlative: afʿal + wāḥid / shay / noun (aḥsan wāḥid, aghla wāḥid, aḥsan shay)
dialogue: السلام عليكم. أبي عطر حق أمي. شو أحسن شي عندك؟
as-salāmu ʿalaykum. abi ʿiṭir ḥagg ummi. shu aḥsan shay ʿindak?
Hello. I want a perfume for my mum. What's the best thing you have?
وعليكم السلام. هذا أحسن واحد عندي، دهن عود
wa ʿalaykum is-salām. hādha aḥsan wāḥid ʿindi, dihn ʿūd
Hello. This is the best one I've got: oud oil.
ما شاء الله، ريحته حلوة. بكم؟
mā shāʼ allāh, rīḥtah ḥilwa. b-cham?
Wow, it smells lovely. How much?
Two hundred. It's the most expensive one here.
That's a bit expensive. What's your best price?
ʿashānak, b-miya w khamsīn. ākhir kalām
For you, a hundred and fifty. That's my last word.
OK, I'll take it. A lovely present!
items: for a feminine thing: aḥsan waḥda
for you, for your sake (to a man)
culture: Bargaining is normal in the old souqs, such as the spice and perfume souqs in Deira, but not in malls and chain shops, where prices are fixed. Oud oil (dihn ʿūd) and bukhūr (incense) are classic Gulf presents.

title: Taking it back
goal: Return a watch that doesn't work to a shop assistant (a woman) and ask for one like your friend's
tip: mithil 'like' goes before a noun or takes an ending: mithil sāʿat rbīʿi 'like my friend's watch', mithilha 'like it (f.)'. Emiratis also say shrāt: shrātha 'just like it'. ishtarēt 'I bought' ends like sawwēt.
grammar: mithil + noun or ending 'like' (mithil sāʿat rbīʿi, mithilha); UAE shrāt
dialogue: مساء الخير. اشتريت هالساعة أمس، بس ما تشتغل
masāʼ il-khēr. ishtarēt has-sāʿa ams, bas ma tishtaghil
Good evening. I bought this watch yesterday, but it doesn't work.
Good evening. Broken? Do you have the receipt?
Yes, here you are. I want to exchange it.
Sure. Do you want another one just like it?
لا، أبي وحدة مثل ساعة ربيعي، أكبر شوي
la, abi waḥda mithil sāʿat rbīʿi, akbar shwayy
No, I want one like my friend's watch, a bit bigger.
That one? It's fifty dirhams more.
items: I bought; you bought (to a man)
to a woman: ishtarēti (اشتريتي); you'll also hear shirēt (شريت)
it doesn't work (a feminine thing: a watch, a car)
for a masculine thing: ma yishtaghil (ما يشتغل)
abi abaddilha = I want to exchange it; for a masculine thing: abaddlah (أبدله)
for a masculine thing: wāḥid thāni
mithilha = like it (f.); mithlah = like it (m.)
the default is mithil (مثل); shrātha = just like it (f.)

title: Splitting the bill
goal: Pay at a café with Sēf: insist on sharing, say how you'll pay, leave the change
tip: Recap: compare places with aḥsan min and arkhaṣ; mithil also makes 'as usual': mithil kill marra. Paying: adfaʿ 'I pay', badfaʿ 'I'll pay', tidfaʿ? 'are you paying?'. nuṣṣ nuṣṣ 'half and half' splits the bill between two.
dialogue: والله الأكل هني أحسن من المول
wallāh il-akil hni aḥsan min il-mōl
Honestly, the food here is better than at the mall.
صح، وأرخص بعد. الحساب لو سمحت!
ṣaḥḥ, w arkhaṣ baʿad. il-ḥsāb law samaḥt!
True, and cheaper too. The bill, please!
لا والله، مثل كل مرة! نص نص
la wallāh, mithil kill marra! nuṣṣ nuṣṣ
No way, that's what you say every time! Let's go halves.
OK. Are you paying cash or card?
بطاقة، ما عندي فلوس في جيبي
biṭāga, ma ʿindi flūs fi jēbi
Card, I don't have any money on me.
عادي، أنا أدفع كاش، وخل الباقي له
ʿādi, ana adfaʿ kāsh, w khall il-bāgi lah
No problem, I'll pay cash and leave him the change.
items: half and half, let's go halves
culture: Friends often argue over the bill (la wallāh! ʿala ḥsābi!), and the one who invited usually pays. Young friends and colleagues also split it (nuṣṣ nuṣṣ). With an elder or at someone's home, let the host pay and thank them.

title: Checkpoint 2.2: a present for Sēf's mum
goal: Call Sēf, who is shopping with Fahad: ask the group what they're doing, compare presents and offer to chip in
tip: To a group, past verbs take -tu (ligētu 'you found') and present verbs -ūn (shu gāʿdīn tsawwūn?). shrāykum? is short for shu raʼykum? 'what do you think?'; before a verb it means 'how about…?': shrāykum nrūḥ? aḥla shay 'the best thing' is a superlative.
grammar: checkpoint 2.2: recycle s2u018–s2u035 (gāʿid, comparatives, superlatives, mithil)
dialogue: Hello Sēf, what are you guys doing?
أنا وفهد في المول، نشتري هدية حق أمي
ana w Fahad fi l-mōl, nishtiri hadiyya ḥagg ummi
Fahad and I are at the mall, buying a present for my mum.
لا، ما اشترينا شي. الساعات هني كلها مثل بعض
la, ma ishtarēna shay. is-sāʿāt hni killaha mithil baʿaẓ
No, we haven't bought anything. The watches here are all the same.
شرايكم نروح سوق العطور في ديرة؟
shrāykum nrūḥ sūg il-ʿuṭūr fi Dēra?
How about we go to the perfume souq in Deira?
فكرة حلوة، بس ما عندي بيزات وايد
fikra ḥilwa, bas ma ʿindi bēzāt wāyid
Good idea, but I haven't got much money.
عادي، أنا بعد بدفع. والعطر أحلى شي!
ʿādi, ana baʿad badfaʿ. w il-ʿiṭir aḥla shay!
No problem, I'll pay too. And perfume is the best thing!
items: to one man: ligēt; ligētu shay? = have you found anything?
ma ishtarēna shay = we haven't bought anything
what do you think? how about…? (to a group)
to one man: shrāyak? (شرايك); to one woman: shrāych? (شرايج)
the best thing, the nicest thing

title: Grandad's old house
goal: Look at an old photo with Sēf and ask what his grandad's house was like
tip: Gulf has no 'is' in the present, but the past needs kān 'was': il-bēt kān ṣghīr. With a feminine subject it's kānat: kānat il-manṭiga hādya. kān fī 'there was', ma kān fī 'there wasn't', kān ʿindi 'I had': here kān doesn't change.
grammar: kān 'was': kān, kānat; kān fī 'there was'; kān ʿind- 'had'
dialogue: شوف، هذا بيت يدي أيام زمان
shūf, hādha bēt yaddi ayyām zamān
Look, this is my grandad's house in the old days.
لا، كان صغير، بس كان في حوش كبير
la, kān ṣghīr, bas kān fī ḥōsh kbīr
No, it was small, but there was a big courtyard.
And did you have air conditioning?
لا والله، ما كان في مكيف. والصيف كان صعب
la wallāh, ma kān fī mkayyif. w iṣ-ṣēf kān ṣaʿb
No, there was no air conditioning. And summer was hard.
في ديرة. كانت المنطقة هادية، الحين زحمة
fi Dēra. kānat il-manṭiga hādya, il-ḥīn zaḥma
In Deira. The area was quiet; now it's packed.
items: kān doesn't change: kān fī ḥōsh
did you have? (to a group or a family)
I had: kān ʿindi; to one man: kān ʿindak?
the old days, back in the day

title: When I was little
goal: Ask Umm Sēf about her childhood and tell her about yours
tip: kān + a present-tense verb means 'used to': kinna nilʿab 'we used to play', kint arūḥ 'I used to go'. Both verbs agree with the subject: kinti trūḥīn? 'did you use to go?' (to a woman). lamma kint ṣghīr 'when I was little' (a woman: ṣghīra).
grammar: kān + present verb = 'used to' (kint arūḥ, kinna nilʿab); lamma 'when'
dialogue: لما كنتي صغيرة، وين كنتي ساكنة؟
lamma kinti ṣghīra, wēn kinti sākna?
When you were little, where did you live?
كنا ساكنين في ديرة، قريب من البحر
kinna sāknīn fi Dēra, garīb min il-baḥar
We lived in Deira, near the sea.
w shu kinti tsawwīn kill yōm?
And what did you use to do every day?
كنا نلعب في الفريج ويا العيال
kinna nilʿab fi l-firīj wiyya l-ʿyāl
We used to play in the neighbourhood with the other kids.
And did you go to school?
هيه، كنت أمشي ويا خواتي. وانت؟
hē, kint amshi wiyya khawāti. w inta?
Yes, I used to walk there with my sisters. And you?
أنا لما كنت صغير، كنت أروح بالباص
ana lamma kint ṣghīr, kint arūḥ bil-bāṣ
When I was little, I used to go by bus.
items: when I was little (said by a man)
a woman says: lamma kint ṣghīra; UAE also: yōm kint ṣghīr (يوم كنت صغير)
I was; you were (to a man)
to a woman: kinti; kint + verb = I used to: kint arūḥ
the neighbourhood (old-style, where families know each other)
culture: Before oil was found in 1966 (first shipped in 1969), many Dubai families lived from the sea: pearling, fishing and trade along the Creek, with Deira on one bank and Bur Dubai on the other. Life centred on the firīj, the neighbourhood where everyone knew each other; the Emirati cartoon Freej (2006) is named after it.

title: Dubai used to be different
goal: Talk with Maryam about how Dubai has changed since she was a child
tip: kān works with comparatives too: kānat iz-zaḥma agall 'the traffic was lighter', awwal kān ahda 'it used to be quieter'. For 'used to', kān agrees with the subject: kintu trūḥūn 'you (all) used to go', kānaw yaʿarfūn 'they used to know'.
grammar: kān + present verb for groups (kintu trūḥūn, kānaw yaʿarfūn); kān + comparative
dialogue: تدري؟ لما كنت صغيرة، ما كان في مترو
tadri? lamma kint ṣghīra, ma kān fī mitro
You know what? When I was little, there was no metro.
والله؟ يعني كنتوا تروحون كل مكان بالسيارة؟
wallāh? yaʿni kintu trūḥūn kill makān bis-sayyāra?
Really? So you all used to go everywhere by car?
هيه، بس الزحمة كانت أقل من الحين
hē, bas iz-zaḥma kānat agall min il-ḥīn
Yes, but there was less traffic than now.
akīd! w in-nās kānaw yaʿarfūn baʿaẓ
Of course! And people used to know each other.
دبي تغيرت وايد. أول كان أحسن؟
Dbayy tghayyarat wāyid. awwal kān aḥsan?
Dubai has changed a lot. Was it better before?
ما أدري. الحين أحسن، بس أول كان أهدى
ma adri. il-ḥīn aḥsan, bas awwal kān ahda
I don't know. Now is better, but before it was quieter.
items: kintu trūḥūn = you used to go (to a group)

title: How long have you been here?
goal: Answer a new Emirati colleague: how long you've been in Dubai and learning Arabic, and whether you're used to it
tip: ṣār-li + a time says how long something has gone on: ṣār-li sana fi Dbayy 'I've been in Dubai a year'. Add a verb for 'have been doing': ṣār-li sitt shhūr atʿallam. Ask with cham: cham ṣār-lak? (to a woman: ṣār-lich).
grammar: ṣār-li + time 'I've been … for': ṣār-li sana; cham ṣār-lak?
dialogue: انت من بريطانيا؟ كم صار لك في دبي؟
inta min Brīṭānya? cham ṣār-lak fi Dbayy?
Are you from Britain? How long have you been in Dubai?
ما شاء الله، وتتكلم عربي زين!
mā shāʼ allāh, w titkallam ʿarabi zēn!
Great, and you speak Arabic well!
شوي شوي. صار لي ست شهور أتعلم
shwayy shwayy. ṣār-li sitt shhūr atʿallam
Little by little. I've been learning for six months.
And have you got used to Dubai?
Yes, but the heat's hard for me.
That's normal, give it two years and you'll get used to it!
items: ṣār-lah = he's been; ṣār-lha = she's been
how long have you been (here)? (to a man)
to a woman: cham ṣār-lich? (كم صار لج)
I've got used to; you've got used to (to a man)
you'll get used to it (to a man)
